Learning Objectives
Assess risk factors and identify patients at a high risk for periprosthetic joint infection after
primary total joint arthroplasty.
Apply preventative measures for periprosthetic joint infection, including best practices for
patient optimization and perioperative care.
Compare various types of periprosthetic joint infections, and implement management based
on acute versus chronic infection.
Discuss the current definition of and determine diagnostic strategies for periprosthetic joint
infection.
Review and identify surgical and nonsurgical treatment options for periprosthetic joint
infection.

Overview
Epidemiology
Periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) is a devastating complication associated with increased
morbidity and mortality and poses an economic burden to the healthcare system.
The risk of PJI after primary total knee arthroplasty (TKA; 1% to 3%) is slightly higher than that
after total hip arthroplasty (THA; 0.5% to 2%).
The risk of PJI is higher after revision procedures: 3% for hips and 6% for knees.

Epidemiology
PJI is a devastating complication that may occur after total joint arthroplasty (TJA) of the
hip or knee. It is a relatively uncommon complication, with a prevalence of
approximately 1% to 3% after primary TKA and 0.5% to 2% after primary THA.1
PJI is associated with substantially increased morbidity and mortality. Management often
consists of multiple revision procedures for to the joint. PJI is the most common cause of
revision TKA (25% of revision TKA procedures) and the third most common cause of
revision THA (15% of revision THA procedures).2,3 Patients with PJI undergo prolonged
hospital stays and experience additional complications and have a substantially
increased short-term and long-term mortality rate compared with patients with an
aseptic TJA implant.4
In addition, PJI is associated with an economic burden on patients and the overall
healthcare system. With an increasing number of primary TJA procedures being
performed, the absolute number and cost of infected arthroplasty implants and
subsequent care has increased in previous decades. In the United States, the annual cost
of revision TJA necessitated by infection is projected to exceed $1.62 billion.5,6

Risk Factors
To identify patients at high risk for PJI and to develop methods to optimize patient
outcomes preoperatively, surgeons must identify all modifiable and nonmodifiable risk
factors. A number of demographic factors, surgical factors, and comorbidities influence
the risk of infection. A validated risk calculator developed by Tan et al7 assigns weighted
values to risk factors to determine a patient’s risk of PJI (Resource 1).
Prevention
Host Factors
Preoperative optimization by addressing all modifiable risk factors
Avoid TJA in patients with an active infection within the joint or from another site (non-articular
infection)

Host Factors
Because TJA is an elective procedure, preoperative optimization of risk factors in high-
risk patients is a critical component of preventing PJI.9 (Video 1)
The presence of an active local or systemic infection predisposes patients to PJI because
of the possibility of hematogenous or direct seeding of the implant after TJA. Therefore,
arthroplasty should be delayed until any active source of infection can be
eradicated.10,11

Native skin flora is a possible source of infection in PJI. To reduce the bacterial load of
this skin flora at the time of surgery, a cleansing of the entire body with the use of
antibacterial soap is recommended. Chlorhexidine, a broad-spectrum bactericidal agent,
is effective against gram-positive and gram-negative organisms. Compared with soap
and water, chlorhexidine has been shown in a randomized controlled trial to reduce the
rate of PJI by sevenfold, and it is the recommended agent for preoperative skin cleansing
the night before and immediately before surgery.12,13
Among patients with rheumatologic diseases and other inflammatory conditions, the use
of corticosteroids, disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs, and biologic antirheumatic
medication increases the risk of PJI. Depending on the medication and underlying
disease, surgeons should work closely with patients and rheumatology colleagues to
determine if and when to withhold certain treatments before surgery based on the half-
life of the medication.8
Perioperative Measures
All patients should be screened for uncontrolled diabetes mellitus preoperatively.
Timely and weight-based administration of effective antibiotic agents (eg, cephalosporin) is
critical for preventing infection.
Minimize the number of people in and the traffic in and out of the operating room.
Wound irrigation with the use of an antiseptic, such as povidone-iodine, is a safe and effective
measure to prevent PJI.

Perioperative Measures
Patients with hyperglycemia at the time of surgery have a substantially increased risk of
surgical site infection and subsequent PJI.14 This has been demonstrated among patients
with uncontrolled diabetes mellitus and among patients without diabetes in whom
hyperglycemia develops. Therefore, all patients should be screened as part of a strict
glycemic protocol at the time of surgery regardless whether a diagnosis of diabetes
mellitus has been made. Guidelines and institutional practices differ slightly with respect

to a glycemic threshold; however, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has
made a strong recommendation for a fasting glucose level of less than 200 mg/dL before
surgery.12,15,16 Investigators in a multicenter study reported that a hemoglobin A1c level
higher than 7.7% was a risk factor for PJI.17
Prophylactic use of antibiotic agents is critical to the prevention of surgical site infection
and PJI. Although the postoperative continuation of prophylaxis continues to be a
subject of debate, it is well documented that the preoperative administration of
antibiotic agents shortly before incision substantially reduces the rate of infection.18,19
The antibiotic agent should demonstrate bactericidal activity against the most common
organisms causing infection, and its administration should be timed such that a
minimum inhibitory concentration is present at the time the first incision is made.20 A
first-generation cephalosporin (eg, cefazolin) is often the first choice, with vancomycin
used in patients with a higher risk for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus
infection.12
The operating room environment has an effect on the rate of PJI. Ambient air in the
operating room is believed to be a route of microbial entry, and strategies to prevent
infection include strict control of the operating room environment. Personnel in the
operating room are the main source of particles in the air, and the number of people
and the number of door openings are known to increase the quantity of bacteria-laden
particles in the air.21 In addition, findings of multiple studies have linked the rate of
operating room traffic to the rate of surgical site infection.22 Therefore, to prevent
infection, operating room traffic should be kept to a minimum during TJA.
Dilute povidone-iodine is a solution that gradually releases free iodine, which is toxic to
potentially pathogenic microorganisms.23 It is used intraoperatively as irrigation before
wound closure as a measure to prevent PJI, is supported by Centers for Disease Control
and Prevention and World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines, and has been proven
to reduce the rate of PJI after primary TJA.15,24-27

Presentation and Etiology
Pain at the implant site is the most common symptom of PJI and is associated with infection in
more than 90% of patients.
A sinus tract with evidence of communication to the joint is considered diagnostic of PJI.
Patients with an acute infection may have overt signs of infection (fever, warmth and redness
of skin overlying joint); however, these signs may be absent in patients with a chronic infection.


The most common presentation of PJI is pain; therefore, infection must be ruled out in
any patient with persistent pain after TJA.32,33 The presence of symptoms other than
pain often depends on the acuity of the infection. Patients with an acute PJI often will
have classic signs of infection, such as erythema, warmth, and tenderness of the skin
overlying the joint and a fever. Chronic infections may be more subtle, without any
systemic signs.
Regardless of acuity, the presence of a sinus tract with communication to the joint is an
examination finding pathognomonic for PJI.
In addition, the pain of a chronic infection may resemble and be confused with that of
mechanical failure. Although diagnostic tests (serum and synovial fluid tests) are
necessary to differentiate PJI from aseptic loosening, the pain associated with chronic
infection worsens with time and is accompanied by deterioration in function. Conversely,
the pain associated with mechanical aseptic loosening often improves with rest.32
Overall, the signs and symptoms of PJI are nonspecific and overlap with those of
hematoma formation, aseptic loosening or prosthesis, or soft-tissue instability.
Therefore, additional workup often is necessary for accurate diagnosis, including serum
and synovial fluid laboratory studies, imaging studies, microbiologic studies,
histopathologic studies, and molecular studies.34

Diagnosis
Definition
Prior Musculoskeletal Infection Society and International Consensus Meeting (ICM) definitions
helped standardize PJI diagnosis.
The updated 2018 ICM definition is a validated and score-based definition that is associated
with a higher sensitivity and incorporates newer diagnostic biomarkers and molecular tests.

Definition
In addition to a careful clinical evaluation of a patient’s history and physical examination
findings, many laboratory tests are used to diagnose PJI. Testing methods and diagnostic
biomarkers and the definition of PJI by which positive results are determined have
evolved in recent years. Researchers continue to investigate the best manner of defining
and diagnosing PJI (Resource 2).
The prior Musculoskeletal Infection Society (MSIS) and ICM definitions helped
standardize PJI diagnosis. In 2018, a multi-institutional effort resulted in a new PJI
diagnostic scoring system (Table 3), which is associated with a sensitivity of 97.7%, an
improvement over that of the prior Musculoskeletal Infection Society and ICM
definitions. The updated schema also incorporates newer diagnostic biomarkers and
molecular tests that were not considered in the earlier definitions.

Scintigraphy involving the use of technetium Tc-99m (which detects inflammation) or indium
In-111 (which detects leukocytes) can be used as an adjunct in the diagnosis of challenging
patients with a chronic low-grade infection.
Positron emission tomography has been shown to have a role in diagnosis, with a high


Imaging Studies
Although radiographs are not highly sensitive or specific for the diagnosis of infection,
they may provide some information regarding the cause of failed TJA and are a crucial
component in preoperative planning. Infection may result in radiographic changes, such
as a periosteal reaction at the bone-cement or bone-prosthesis interface, scattered foci
of osteolysis, and generalized bone resorption in the absence of implant wear.35 Figure
1 demonstrates these findings.
For patients in whom infection is clinically suspected but cannot be confirmed, additional
imaging studies may be warranted. Bone, leukocyte, bone marrow, and antigranulocyte
scintigraphy may play a role in the diagnosis of PJI.36 These studies involve the use of
radioactive tracers, such as technetium Tc-99m, which detects inflammation, and indium
In-111, which detects leukocytes in periprosthetic tissue. In three-phase bone
scintigraphy, images are obtained throughout the three phases: perfusion, blood pool,
and late phase (depicting osteoblastic activity). A recent meta-analysis reported that
bone scintigraphy is associated with a very high sensitivity (93%) and, therefore, can be
used to rule out infection.37 However, the technique is limited by a low specificity
because a positive finding may result from any increase in osteoblast activity, including
PJI, physiologic bone remodeling, or aseptic loosening.36,37
Fluorodeoxyglucose–positron emission tomography also has been shown to play a role
in the diagnosis of PJI. The advantages of positron emission tomography over
scintigraphy include time efficiency, increased resolution, and use of low-dose CT.36
Positron emission tomography is associated with a relatively high sensitivity and

Serologic Tests
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and serum C-reactive protein (CRP) levels are nonspecific
markers of inflammation used as initial screening tools in the diagnosis of PJI.
Interleukin-6 (IL-6) is a cytokine produced by activated monocytes and macrophages as part of
the inflammatory response.
D-dimer is a fibrin degradation product released in blood after fibrin clot breakdown by
plasmin that is elevated in patients with PJI.
Fibrinogen is another serum marker of infection that is elevated in patients with PJI.

Serologic Tests
Serum ESR and CRP levels are nonspecific markers of inflammation that, in combination,
are very useful as an initial screening tool in the diagnosis of infection. Both laboratory
tests are low-cost, widely available, and noninvasive.38 A combined ESR greater than 30
mm/hr and a CRP level greater than>10mg/L has been traditionally believed to be
associated with a high sensitivity for the diagnosis of PJI. The CRP level measured should
not be cardiac or high-sensitivity CRP. The sensitivity of these tests has been questioned
in recent years, with a false-positive rate as high as 11.1% for combined ESR and CRP
level.39 This is especially true in patients with indolent, chronic infections caused by
slow-growing organisms, for which a sufficient inflammatory response is not mounted to
increase these markers. Therefore, other serum tests recently have been explored.
ESR and CRP levels also are less reliable in patients in whom an acute postoperative
infection is suspected. CRP levels normalize within 21 days postoperatively, whereas 90
days may be required for ESR to normalize. Continued high CRP levels and ESR should
elicit concern for possible infection. ESR and CRP levels also are unreliable in patients
with inflammatory conditions, including rheumatoid arthritis and psoriatic arthritis.

IL-6 may be a faster and more sensitive laboratory marker for the detection of PJI
because it lies upstream of other markers in the acute phase inflammatory cascade.40
Serum levels of IL-6 return to normal (<1 pg/mL) within approximately 2 to 3 days of
uncomplicated arthroplasty. Because of wide variation in IL-6 levels with an unknown
threshold, lack of easy accessibility, and cost, IL-6 testing has not yet gained widespread
adoption.
D-dimer, a fibrin degradation product, is a nonspecific marker often used to aid in
screening for venous thromboembolism. It also has shown promise as a biomarker for
diagnosis of PJI and determining optimal time for reimplantation in patients undergoing
two-stage exchange arthroplasty. D-dimer has been demonstrated to outperform ESR
and CRP level with regard to diagnostic accuracy.41 Similar to IL-6, D-dimer returns to
baseline levels more quickly postoperatively than ESR and CRP levels; however, D-dimer
testing is associated with much lower costs and is widely available.44, 45, 46
Fibrinogen is enzymatically converted by thrombin to fibrin and contributes to clot
formation. Compared with D-dimer, fibrinogen has a higher area under the curve (0.852),
with an optimal threshold of 4.01g/L for the diagnosis of PJI.47
Synovial Fluid Tests
Joint fluid aspiration is performed in patients in whom infection is strongly suspected. Synovial
fluid should be evaluated for bacterial and fungal culture and for biomarkers.
Synovial fluid white blood cell (WBC) count and polymorphonuclear neutrophil (PMN)
percentage are established tests for the diagnosis of PJI, with different thresholds for acute
postoperative and chronic infections.
Leukocyte esterase is an enzyme produced by activated neutrophils. It can be measured with
the use of a colorimetric chemical strip and is a low-cost, semiquantitative, point-of-service test
that is 81% sensitive and 100% specific for the diagnosis of PJI.
Alpha defensin is a naturally occurring antimicrobial peptide released from activated
neutrophils as part of the innate immune response to pathogens. It is associated with
excellent sensitivity and specificity that is unaffected by previous antibiotic administration
even with low-virulence organisms.


Synovial Fluid Tests
Joint fluid aspiration is performed if infection is suspected. Traditionally, synovial fluid
was obtained only to analyze for bacterial culture.48 However, multiple biomarkers
present in the synovial fluid are highly sensitive and specific for the diagnosis of PJI, and
they are included as minor criteria in the ICM definition of PJI. Therefore, evaluation of
the joint via aspiration is an important component of diagnosis.
WBC and PMN percentage are established tests that aid in the diagnosis of PJI,
demonstrating high sensitivity (89%) and high specificity (86%).48 For acute PJI (<6 weeks
postoperatively), a threshold of 12,800 WBC/μL and a PMN percentage of 89% ( is
indicative of hip PJI,49 and a threshold of 27,800 WBC/μL and a PMN percentage of 89%
is indicative of knee PJI.50 For chronic PJI (>6 weeks postoperatively), a threshold of
greater than 3,000 WBC/μL and a PMN percentage higher than 80% is indicative of PJI.
False-negative results may result from improper technique, low-virulence or biofilm-
producing organisms, or antibiotic therapy at the time of aspiration. False-positive
results may result from contamination, which can be avoided with the use of more
sterile technique. In addition, a false-positive result may be observed in patients with an
adverse local tissue reaction because monocyte-phagocytosed metal particles may be
interfering with laboratory instruments; a manual synovial WBC count is recommended
in these patients.51
The leukocyte esterase colorimetric chemical strip, previously used to diagnose urinary
tract infection, is a low-cost, semiquantitative, point-of-service test that is 81% sensitive
and 97% specific for the diagnosis of PJI; Because blood within the synovial fluid may
interfere with the color change of the urine analysis strip, a centrifuge must be used to
ensure removal of blood contamination.42
Alpha defensin is a naturally occurring antimicrobial peptide released from activated
neutrophils as part of the innate immune response to pathogens. Alpha defensin rises in
response to low-virulence organisms and is unaffected by prior antibiotic administration.

Microbiology
A definitive diagnosis can be made if the same pathogen is recovered via serial joint aspiration
or from at least two specimens of periprosthetic tissue obtained intraoperatively.
A single positive culture may represent contamination and should be considered in
combination with other serum and synovial fluid markers of infection.

Microbiology
A definitive diagnosis of PJI can be made if two positive cultures of the same pathogen
are recovered via serial joint aspirate or intraoperative culture.
Synovial fluid obtained preoperatively, intraoperatively, or both should be analyzed for
WBC count, neutrophil differential, and other biomarkers, as well as for culture.
However, the microorganisms causing infection in patients with PJI are mostly adherent
to the implant as part of a biofilm, with a much smaller quantity of bacteria existing in
the planktonic state to be identified in synovial fluid. Therefore, the sensitivity of synovial
fluid culture is limited, and the collection of multiple intraoperative tissue samples is
considered higher yield.56 Gram stains should be avoided in the diagnosis of PJI.57 - 59
At least three intraoperative culture samples should be obtained. The optimal number of
intraoperative samples is likely higher, especially if the likely pathogen is unknown.
Findings of one study demonstrated that five samples provided the highest yield.60 With
the increase in numbers of biofilm-producing and slow-growing, fastidious organisms
(eg, Propionibacterium acnes), techniques for improving the accuracy of PJI diagnosis

Histopathology
Histologic analysis of periprosthetic tissue is another valuable tool that aids in the diagnosis of
PJI.
The presence of PMN infiltrate on histologic images closely correlates with PJI.
Frozen sections are used for intraoperative assessment, and paraffin sections are used for
final postoperative assessment.

Histopathology
Histologic analysis of periprosthetic tissue is another valuable tool for the diagnosis of
PJI. The presence of PMN infiltrate on histologic images closely correlates with PJI and is
considered a minor criterion in the ICM definition of PJI.61 The criterion considered to be
diagnostic is more than 5 neutrophils per high-power field in five high-power fields at a
magnification of ́400.
Histologic images are most useful in equivocal cases in which preoperative investigations
are confounded by false increases in ESR and CRP levels or if the intraoperative
appearance of the joint may indicate infection. In these patients, frozen sections can be
used for intraoperative assessment, and paraffin sections can be obtained for definitive
postoperative diagnosis.61
Molecular Techniques
Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) uses the amplification of regions of bacterial DNA to identify
pathogens.
The sensitivity of PCR likely is greater than that of culture, but it is still limited by a panel of
primer targets.

Molecuar Techniques
Even in patients in whom PJI is confirmed via serum and synovial biomarkers, accurate
identification of the organism causing PJI is not always possible via traditional culture.
Even with strategies to optimize yield, culture fails to identify any organism in as many as
50% of patients with an infection.62,63 The choice of antimicrobial therapy is imprecise in
these patients, which is associated with an increased risk of failure compared with
culture-positive PJI.64
PCR has been investigated as a culture-independent technology to diagnose and identify
pathogens in patients with PJI. It amplifies bacterial DNA based on a set of primer targets
from common pathogens. The sensitivity of PCR is likely greater than that of traditional
culture. It also has shown success in identifying the genes responsible for antibiotic
resistance, which is necessary in guiding appropriate management.63 However,
considerable limitations have prevented its widespread clinical use. Importantly, PCR
requires a panel of primer targets and, therefore, is restricted in the organisms it can
identify.

Management
General Treatment Principles
Management of PJI usually involves multiple procedures and a prolonged course of
antimicrobial therapy.
Biofilm is characteristic of PJI and is believed to form and establish within 4 weeks
postoperatively, which presents a challenge in the diagnosis and eradication of PJI. For
established infections, prosthesis removal is recommended.
Early postoperative and acute hematogenous infections are less likely to be associated with
biofilm formation and less likely to require prosthesis removal.
Surgical management
Two-stage exchange arthroplasty is the preferred method for the management of chronic PJI.
Irrigation and débridement with retention of the prosthesis is potentially effective for
infections occurring within 4 to 6 weeks of index arthroplasty or after an inciting event, such
as dental extraction in a healthy host.
Nonsurgical management
Suppressive antimicrobial therapy may be administered to patients who refuse surgical
treatment and patients in whom surgical treatment is contraindicated because of their
general medical condition; however, its use is rare.

Two-Stage Exchange Arthroplasty
In patients with chronic PJI, pathogens on the implant surface develop resistance to
antimicrobial therapy as a result of biofilm formation. Prosthesis removal is necessary to
eradicate infection, and two-stage exchange arthroplasty is considered the standard of
care for most patients.66 Two-stage exchange arthroplasty includes resection of the
implants, débridement of the joint, placement of a temporary ALBC spacer, and
reimplantation of a prosthesis after eradication of infection (Resource 3).
After removal of the prosthesis and adequate débridement of infected tissue, ALBC
spacers (non-articulating or articulating) often are used in the interim before
reimplantation (Figure 3). Spacers are used to reduce dead space, provide joint stability,
and deliver high local doses of antimicrobial agents.

with the use of a dynamic spacer; however, the clinical effects on function are unclear.67
After resection arthroplasty and placement of an ALBC spacer, systemic antimicrobial
agents are administered until reimplantation. The interval between the removal of a
prosthesis and reimplantation varies, and no conclusive evidence has determined the
optimal timing of reimplantation. However, evidence suggests that spacers should be
retained for at least 4 weeks.68
Initial empiric therapy for most common pathogens is a first-generation cephalosporin
or vancomycin in patients with a history or suspicion of methicillin-resistant S aureus
infection. After identification of the pathogen and susceptibility results, the antibiotic
regimen should be tailored to the findings. (Video 4)
Traditionally, studies recommended the cessation of antimicrobial therapy for at least 2
weeks before joint fluid aspiration and repeat serologies; however, recent evidence
suggests that this antibiotic holiday is unnecessary.69
The proper timing of reimplantation after parenteral antibiotic therapy should be based
on the clinical appearance of the wound and improvement in serologic markers of
infection, such as CRP level and ESR. At the time of reimplantation, tissue specimens
should be sent for culture with or without histopathologic evaluation. Reimplantation is
indicated in patients in whom all preoperative and intraoperative indices are acceptable.
If a frozen-tissue section indicates continued acute inflammation, then débridement of
the wound should be repeated, and a new cement spacer should be placed. (Video 5)

In a subset of patients with known organisms, a good host with minimal comorbidities, and a
viable soft-tissue envelope with primary implants, single-stage exchange arthroplasty may

Healthy soft tissues that can be closed over a new prosthesis

Débridement With Retention of Prosthesis
In patients with an early postoperative PJI or acute hematogenous PJI, the organisms
causing infection may not yet have formed a biofilm. Compared with chronic PJI,
débridement, antibiotic agents, and implant retention will succeed in eradicating the
infection without the need for exchange arthroplasty.
Management should take place within 1 week of the onset of symptoms for the
maximum likelihood of success.73, 74 All infected tissue should be débrided, and high-
volume irrigation should be performed. Modular components (eg, polyethylene insert)
should be exchanged if possible, because removal allows for better visualization for
débridement of infected tissue. Exchange of modular components at the time of
débridement has been demonstrated to prolong implant survival and decrease the risk
of reinfection.74
Even in patients with acute PJI, treatment via débridement, antibiotic agents, and implant
retention is associated with disadvantages and should be used with caution. Severe
infections in patients with a high CRP level or evidence of bacteremia and infections
caused by S aureus or Enterococcus are more likely to result in prosthesis failure after
débridement, the administration of antibiotic agents, and implant retention.75 In
addition, initial irrigation and débridement may compromise the ultimate success of
two-stage exchange arthroplasty, with some studies reporting increased failure rates in
patients who subsequently undergo two-stage exchange artrhoplasty.70

Resection Arthroplasty
Definitive resection arthroplasty without planned reimplantation is a treatment option
for some patients with PJI. If multiple exchange arthroplasty procedures fail to eradicate
an infection, it is unlikely that additional attempts will succeed. Treatment options for
such patients include resection arthroplasty, arthrodesis, and amputation.
In the hip, a Girdlestone resection arthroplasty involves removal of the hip prosthesis
without a replacement. The procedure often is successful in controlling infection, with a
success rate ranging from 73% to 100%.77 However, functional outcomes often are
impaired by limb shortening, hip instability, and the need for a walking aid.78
Resection arthroplasty of the knee is less common because arthrodesis or amputation
often are the preferred treatment options. One recent study reported a success rate of
84% in eradicating infection, concluding that resection arthroplasty is safe and effective
compared with alternative treatment options for the management of recalcitrant PJI of
the knee.79

Nonsurgical Management
The goal in the management of PJI usually is eradication of the infection, and surgical
treatment is almost always necessary to achieve that goal. However, in some patients,
surgical treatment may not be indicated because of comorbidities or refusal of surgery.
In patients with a well-fixed prosthesis, lack of wound drainage, and an infecting
pathogen that is responsive to antibiotic agents, nonsurgical treatment via long-term
suppressive antibiotic agents may be considered to relieve symptoms, maintain joint
function, and prevent the systemic spread of infection.83 However, the likelihood of
infection eradication via nonsurgical management is low. Relapse of infection occurs in
more than 80% of patients who discontinue antimicrobial therapy.84
